<!-- Section 2: Rigorous Mathematical Theory -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-theory">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">01 · Theoretical Mechanics</div>
<h2>1.1 Governing Equation of Motion</h2>
<p>Consider a front-loading washing machine of total assembly mass $M$. Inside the drum, an off-center wet laundry clump of unbalance mass $m_0$ rotates at radius $e$ with angular spin velocity $\omega = 2\pi f$. The suspension system provides equivalent lateral stiffness $k$ and viscous dissipation $c$.</p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<div class="card-title">Newtonian Dynamic Balance</div>
<p>
The horizontal position of the main housing is $x(t)$, while the absolute horizontal coordinate of the eccentric lump is $x_m(t) = x(t) + e \sin(\omega t)$. Applying Newton's second law:
</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$(M - m_0) \ddot{x}(t) + m_0 \frac{d^2}{dt^2}[x(t) + e \sin(\omega t)] + c \dot{x}(t) + k x(t) = 0$$
</div>

<p>
Expanding the second derivative $\frac{d^2}{dt^2}[e \sin(\omega t)] = -e \omega^2 \sin(\omega t)$ and regrouping yields the standard forced vibration ODE:
</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$M \ddot{x}(t) + c \dot{x}(t) + k x(t) = m_0 e \omega^2 \sin(\omega t)$$
</div>

<p>
Normalizing by total mass $M$, we define the undamped natural frequency $\omega_n = \sqrt{k/M}$ and viscous damping ratio $\zeta = \frac{c}{2\sqrt{k M}}$:
</p>

<div class="eq-box">
$$\ddot{x}(t) + 2\zeta \omega_n \dot{x}(t) + \omega_n^2 x(t) = \left(\frac{m_0 e}{M}\right) \omega^2 \sin(\omega t)$$
</div>

<div class="callout-note">
<div class="callout-title">Mathematical Derivation · Steady-State Amplitude & Phase</div>
<p>
Assuming steady-state harmonic response of the form $x_p(t) = X \sin(\omega t - \phi)$ and substituting into the ODE yields the exact amplitude and phase relations:
</p>
$$X = \left(\frac{m_0 e}{M}\right) \frac{r^2}{\sqrt{(1 - r^2)^2 + (2\zeta r)^2}} = \left(\frac{m_0 e}{M}\right) M_d(r)$$
$$\phi(r) = \arctan\left(\frac{2\zeta r}{1 - r^2}\right)$$
<p>Where $r = \omega / \omega_n$ is the non-dimensional frequency ratio. Notice that as $r \to \infty$, $M_d(r) \to 1$. Consequently, $X \to \frac{m_0 e}{M}$, meaning the machine naturally spins about its combined center of mass!</p>
</div>
</div>
</section>

<div class="callout" style="margin-top: 16px; margin-bottom: 0;">
<strong>Physical Takeaway:</strong> Notice that for $r < 1$ (sub-resonant), displacement and unbalance are in-phase ($\phi \to 0^\circ$). At resonance ($r = 1$), the displacement lags by exactly $90^\circ$. For high spin speeds ($r > \sqrt{2}$), the displacement lags by nearly $180^\circ$, causing the heavy housing to shift opposite to the unbalance mass, achieving natural vibration isolation ($T_r < 1$)!
</div>
</div>

<!-- Section 4: Pedagogical Misconception Callout -->
<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-misconceptions">
<div class="callout-important">
<div class="callout-title">
<svg width="20" height="20" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><path d="M10.29 3.86L1.82 18a2 2 0 0 0 1.71 3h16.94a2 2 0 0 0 1.71-3L13.71 3.86a2 2 0 0 0-3.42 0z"/><line x1="12" y1="9" x2="12" y2="13"/><line x1="12" y1="17" x2="12.01" y2="17"/></svg>
Common Misconception · Adding More Damping Is Always Better?
</div>
<p style="margin: 0 0 8px 0;">
A frequent engineering mistake is assuming that increasing damping $\zeta$ always reduces vibrations.
</p>
<p style="margin: 0;">
While higher damping reduces peak amplitude during the brief pass through resonance ($r = 1$), <strong>it actually increases the force transmitted to the floor at high operating spin speeds ($r > \sqrt{2}$)</strong>! In the isolation zone ($r > \sqrt{2}$), stiff viscous dampers transmit high-frequency shock forces directly into the base structure. Modern washing machine designs use speed-dependent dampers or tuned spring suspensions to balance resonance traversal against high-speed quietness.
</p>
</div>
</section>

<section class="lesson-section" id="sec-code">
<div class="section-header">
<div class="section-tag">04 · Computational Implementation</div>
<h2>1.4 Numerical Simulation in Python & MATLAB</h2>
<p>Execute and reproduce these exact dynamic response curves using the verified algorithms below.</p>
</div>

<div class="code-box">
<div class="code-header">
<div class="code-tabs">
<button class="code-tab-btn active">Python (NumPy / SciPy)</button>
<button class="code-tab-btn">MATLAB</button>
</div>
<button class="btn-copy">Copy Code</button>
</div>
<pre class="code-block"><code>import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Mechanical System Parameters
M = 50.0      # Total machine mass (kg)
m0 = 1.5      # Eccentric unbalance mass (kg)
e = 0.25      # Unbalance radius (m)
fn = 5.0      # Natural frequency (Hz)
wn = 2 * np.pi * fn
zeta = 0.08   # Viscous damping ratio

# Non-dimensional frequency sweep
r = np.linspace(0.1, 3.5, 600)
omega = r * wn

# Dynamic Magnification Factor & Force Transmissibility
denom = np.sqrt((1 - r**2)**2 + (2 * zeta * r)**2)
Md = (r**2) / denom
Tr = np.sqrt(1 + (2 * zeta * r)**2) / denom
phi = np.arctan2(2 * zeta * r, 1 - r**2)

print(f"Resonance peak (r=1): Md = {1 / (2 * zeta):.2f}")
print(f"High-speed spin cycle limit (r -> inf): Md = 1.00 (X = {m0*e/M*1000:.1f} mm)")</code></pre>
<pre class="code-block" hidden><code>% MATLAB Implementation
M = 50.0;     % Total mass (kg)
m0 = 1.5;     % Eccentric mass (kg)
e = 0.25;     % Radius (m)
fn = 5.0;     % Natural frequency (Hz)
wn = 2*pi*fn;
zeta = 0.08;  % Damping ratio

r = linspace(0.1, 3.5, 600);
denom = sqrt((1 - r.^2).^2 + (2*zeta*r).^2);
Md = (r.^2) ./ denom;
Tr = sqrt(1 + (2*zeta*r).^2) ./ denom;

figure;
plot(r, Md, 'LineWidth', 2, 'Color', [0.7, 0.38, 0.16]); grid on;
xlabel('Frequency Ratio r = \omega/\omega_n'); ylabel('Dynamic Magnification M_d');
title('1-DOF Rotating Unbalance Frequency Response');</code></pre>
</div>
